tier_reason: First-party wrk CSVs in benchmarks/results (request_wrk_results.csv for Mach at commit de36047, request_wrk_results_csharp.csv and request_wrk_results_drogon.csv at commit 34c12a4) with the runner benchmarks/runner/request_runner.py public, but no source for the C# or Drogon servers, no hardware, no compiler or flags; partial methodology from the project itself is tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No faster-than claim is made; README says only 'designed to provide high HTTP throughput' and links machframework.dev/benchmarks (EGRESS_BLOCKED, not opened). The repo CSVs cover 7 wrk configs x 6 routes (42 rows per server). Against the file labelled 'csharp', Mach is faster on 20 of 42 rows and slower on 22 (derived from page data): at 16 threads / 100 connections plain 280385.96 vs 100290.9 req/s (2.80x), headers 280097 vs 221091.36 (1.27x), cookies 280342.45 vs 234736.06 (1.19x), body 156975.64 vs 101549.67 (1.55x), small JSON binding 280337.85 vs 253793.28 (1.10x), large JSON binding 149575.36 vs 307173.48 (0.49x); but at 1 thread / 1 connection and 2 threads / 10 connections the C# server is faster on every route (Mach 0.22x to 0.71x, e.g. plain 1/1 29137.3 vs 51441.04 req/s, 0.57x), and it wins every large-binding row. Against the file labelled 'drogon', Mach is slower on all 42 rows (Mach 0.13x to 0.65x; plain 16/100 280385.96 vs 1072586.17 req/s, Drogon 3.83x faster; derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Weak and mixed evidence. (1) Mach publishes no claim of beating any named baseline; the only comparison data are two CSVs (request_wrk_results_csharp.csv and request_wrk_results_drogon.csv) with no server source, no versions, no hardware, no compiler flags. (2) The Mach rows (request_wrk_results.csv, commit de36047, 2026-08-11T00:26) and the comparison rows (commit 34c12a4, 2026-08-11T11:57 and 13:26) are from different runs and may not share a machine or build. (3) Handler work in the comparison servers is unknown; Mach's 'plain' route returns 204 no content. (4) The C# 'win' is selective: Mach beats the C# file only at 4 or more wrk threads (20 of 42 rows) and loses every 1-thread and 2-thread row and every large-JSON-binding row; Mach's own throughput plateaus at about 280k to 292k req/s from 4 threads up while the C# server falls off at 16 threads, which on a loopback run suggests client/server CPU contention rather than a framework difference (inference, not measured). (5) Drogon, the C++ incumbent, is 1.53x to 7.60x faster than Mach on every one of the 42 rows (derived from page data). (6) Website results page machframework.dev/benchmarks could not be opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED). Not evidence that Mach is faster than the C++ incumbent; 4 stars.

notes: CSV numbers in the record are exact, but the record quotes only the 16-thread/100-connection rows: the C# server beats Mach on all 1-thread and 2-thread rows and on every large-binding row (Mach wins 20 of 42), and Drogon beats Mach on all 42 rows. Shortcomings: not faster than the C++ incumbent (Drogon), mixed against an unidentified C# server with no source, first-party, no hardware or flags, 4 stars. Metadata checked: MIT, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-27, active.

tier_reason: The 18% figure is the muduo author's own 2010 blog conclusion (blog.csdn.net/solstice/article/details/5864889, not opened), quoted verbatim by the evpp page; the evpp page itself measures muduo against evpp, not libevent2, so muduo vs libevent2 rests on first-party numbers without verifiable methodology.

corrections.caveats: The 18% figure comes from the author's 2010 CSDN blog post 'muduo与libevent2吞吐量对比' (blog.csdn.net/solstice/article/details/5864889, not opened) and is seen only as quoted by the evpp project's benchmark page ('muduo吞吐量平均比libevent2高 18% 以上'), so hardware, compiler and per-row numbers for muduo vs libevent2 are not verified; tier C, first-party. Benchmark code for both sides is public (chenshuo/recipes pingpong/libevent with Makefile CFLAGS -g -Wall -O2; muduo examples/pingpong built with BUILD_TYPE=release ./build.sh), but the build flags of the published run are unknown, and the libevent2 in the 2010 post is a 2.0.x release. Indirect third-party support only: Qihoo360's evpp docs, on one machine (Xeon E5-2630 v2, CentOS 6.2, gcc 4.8.2, public ping-pong code), show muduo-v1.0.9 roughly equal to evpp-v0.2.4 (each wins some rows) and, in a separate report, evpp 17% to 130% faster than libevent-2.0.21's own server.c/client.c; muduo vs libevent2 was never measured directly there. muduo is a general reactor-style TCP network library (with only an example HTTP server), so the comparison is an event-loop/echo throughput test, not an HTTP framework benchmark. Last commit 2025-02-28 is an issue-template update; the last code change is 2022-11-01.

notes: 18% claim matches the evpp page's quotation of the author's blog (blog URL 5864889 is correct; 5848547 is the muduo intro post). Shortcomings: first-party only, original post unreachable, 2010-era libevent 2.0.x baseline, echo throughput rather than HTTP, evpp's third-party data only transitively supports muduo over libevent2. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause (License file), 16.3k stars, not a fork, stale (last commit 2025-02-28; last code commit 2022-11-01).

corrections.caveats: Unverified, snippet only: the PDF ('Benchmarking for HTTP/2' by Kit Chan, Kenny Peng and Nora Shoemaker of Yahoo, Apache wiki attachments 56066455 and 62696116) could not be opened (cwiki.apache.org and cwiki-test.apache.org blocked), and the verifier's WebSearch excerpts of the deck stop before any CPU utilization or nghttpx results, so the ATS 18% vs nghttpx 15% peak system CPU figures (and the idle figures) are not confirmed by any source opened. Even if correct, they measure CPU utilization at fixed load, not requests per second or latency, a 3-percentage-point efficiency difference against a 2015-era ATS HTTP/2 implementation; hardware, versions and flags unknown. The nghttp2 README's own h2load example (129658 req/s on localhost) is a tool demo with no comparison. An Apache wiki note (snippet only) calls the 2015 ATS HTTP/2 code 50% slower than its HTTPS path and suggests ATS learn from nghttpx's data structures, which is directional only. Kept because nghttp2 is widely used (libnghttp2 is curl's HTTP/2 backend), not because a speed win is shown.

notes: No number could be verified: the PDF host is blocked and search excerpts end before the results, so the entry falls to tier D (if the PDF is opened from another environment and the CPU figures hold, it could return to C or B as a measurement by the baseline's own maintainers at Yahoo). Shortcomings: unverifiable snippet-only evidence, CPU-utilization metric rather than throughput, 2015-era baseline, no comparison in the repo.
